pairs.question: Cur huic genus acre leonum praebent insolitas ad iuga curva iubas?
pairs.answer: Feritas mollita per illam creditur; id curru testificata suo est.
pairs.derivation: Poet asks the Muse why lions yield their manes to the Great Mother's curved yoke. Framing narration 'desierat; coepi:' before the question and 'desieram; coepit:' before the answer is dropped as speech-tag scaffolding. Inline verse numbers 215 stripped. Answer is the Muse's complete two-line reply.

pairs.question: Unde venit sua membra secandi impetus?
pairs.answer: Phryx puer in silvis, facie spectabilis, Attis turrigeram casto vinxit amore deam; hunc sibi servari voluit, sua templa tueri, et dixit "semper fac puer esse velis." Ille fidem iussis dedit, et "si mentiar", inquit "ultima, qua fallam, sit Venus illa mihi." Fallit, et in nympha Sagaritide desinit esse quod fuit: hinc poenas exigit ira deae. Naida volneribus succidit in arbore factis, illa perit; fatum Naidos arbor erat; hic furit, et credens thalami procumbere tectum effugit, et cursu Dindyma summa petit; et modo "tolle faces", "remove" modo "verbera" clamat, saepe Palaestinas iurat adesse deas. Ille etiam saxo corpus laniavit acuto, longaque in immundo pulvere tracta coma est, voxque fuit "merui: meritas do sanguine poenas. Ah pereant partes quae nocuere mihi!" "Ah pereant" dicebat adhuc; onus inguinis aufert, nullaque sunt subito signa relicta viri. Venit in exemplum furor hic, mollesque ministri caedunt iactatis vilia membra comis.
pairs.derivation: Poet asks the Muse (Pieris) the origin of the self-mutilation rite. Framing 'unde venit dixi ... impetus? ut tacui, Pieris orsa loqui:' is split by the speech tag 'dixi'; the question proper is 'unde venit sua membra secandi impetus?' with the tag dropped. Answer is the Muse's full Attis narrative (the aetiology), ending at the line before the closing narration 'talibus Aoniae facunda voce Camenae reddita quaesiti causa furoris erat.' which is excluded as meta-narration. Inline verse numbers 225, 230, 235, 240 stripped; editorial tildes around Palaestinas removed keeping the word.

pairs.question: Hoc quoque, dux operis, moneas precor, unde petita venerit; an nostra semper in urbe fuit?
pairs.answer: Dindymon et Cybelen et amoenam fontibus Iden semper et Iliacas Mater amavit opes: cum Troiam Aeneas Italos portaret in agros, est dea sacriferas paene secuta rates, sed nondum fatis Latio sua numina posci senserat, adsuetis substiteratque locis. Post, ut Roma potens opibus iam saecula quinque vidit et edomito sustulit orbe caput, carminis Euboici fatalia verba sacerdos inspicit; inspectum tale fuisse ferunt: "mater abest: matrem iubeo, Romane, requiras. Cum veniet, casta est accipienda manu."
pairs.derivation: Poet asks whether the Great Mother was always in Rome or was brought from elsewhere; the direct interrogative 'an nostra semper in urbe fuit?' carries the question. Answer is the Muse's reply giving the origin: that the goddess always loved her Phrygian seats and only later came to Rome via the Sibylline oracle. Window ends at the close of the oracle's command (260, '...casta est accipienda manu.'), before the narrative continues with the senators puzzling over the oracle; this first segment genuinely answers the where/whether question. Inline verse numbers 250, 255, 260 stripped.

pairs.question: Cur igitur Gallos qui se excidere vocamus, cum tanto a Phrygia Gallica distet humus?
pairs.answer: Inter viridem Cybelen altasque Celaenas amnis it insana, nomine Gallus, aqua. Qui bibit inde, furit: procul hinc discedite, quis est cura bonae mentis: qui bibit inde, furit.
pairs.derivation: Poet asks why the self-castrated priests are called 'Galli' though Gaul is far from Phrygia. Answer is the goddess's complete reply (the river Gallus aetiology). Speech tag 'ait' within the answer is the author's narration interleaving the quote; here the answer is quoted as the contiguous utterance and 'ait' belongs to the answer line as printed ('inter' ait 'viridem...') — the framing 'ait' is dropped, leaving the contiguous utterance. Inline verse number 365 stripped.

pairs.question: Non pudet herbosum posuisse moretum in dominae mensis? An sua causa subest?
pairs.answer: Lacte mero veteres usi narrantur et herbis, sponte sua siquas terra ferebat, candidus elisae miscetur caseus herbae, cognoscat priscos ut dea prisca cibos.
pairs.derivation: Poet asks whether there is a reason for setting an herb-salad (moretum) on the goddess's table; the direct interrogative 'an sua causa subest?' carries the question. The framing speech tag 'dixi' (printed as 'non pudet herbosum' dixi 'posuisse moretum') is dropped, and 'herbosum' modifies moretum but is split by the tag; the contiguous utterance with the tag removed reads 'non pudet herbosum posuisse moretum in dominae mensis: an sua causa subest?' Answer is the goddess's full reply explaining the ancient diet of milk and herbs; the framing 'ait' is dropped. Inline verse number 370 stripped.
